author: Reel Ken
title: Let me start by stating that this isn't going to be your typ
text:
Let me start by stating that this isn't going to be your typical Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) article. I'm not going to speculate on revenues, iPhone sales, the costs of rare earth metals or rumors about upcoming releases. I'm not going to fill it with charts and graphs of moving averages or say things like "due for a pullback". I'm not going to suggest why one should buy or why one should sell AAPL.
There are more than enough articles and pundits talking about that stuff. There are three, four or more articles each day on Seeking Alpha alone. If you own or want to buy AAPL, you can easily find confirmation of why you should. If you are short or are thinking of selling, you can easily find confirmation of why you should. AAPL articles are so ubiquitous, someone is always right. You just need to pick the right one.
No, this isn't about " whys " - it's simply about how to own AAPL. 
Seasoned AAPL traders will probably get very little from this. That's o.k. I'm an investor, not a trader.
With that said, let's start with the genesis of this article. A common premise running through my articles is that investors should be invested 100% in the market 24/7/365 and hedge with put options for the downside. This flies in the face of those that promote traditional asset allocation models. My premise is based upon the following reasoning:
Stocks consistently outperform cash/bonds over the long run. Investors react emotionally and execute poorly and underperform the asset allocation models anyway. They are motivated by fear and greed, not rational choices. Some studies have put this "emotional loss" at upwards of 300 basis points per year. Wow! When interest rates are low and puts are cheap, hedging with puts is favored over hedging through asset allocation using cash/bonds. It's investing along the lines of "Hope for the best but plan for the worst".
In my latest article , one reader asked an important question: "Can these same hedging techniques be applied to individual stocks, especially high-beta stocks, rather than just at the portfolio level?" This article will attempt to answer that question.
